[Presenter 2 · 0:20]
Why did half the rows disappear? Every variant is listed once per DNA map, so keeping one map removes the copy. Then drop duplicates on Variation ID removed 2,420 more repeats. Without these two steps, every count we report would be doubled.

[Presenter 2 · 0:30]
Next, missing values. Pandas said nothing was missing, because ClinVar writes codes like a dash, 'na' or 'not provided' instead. We counted 2.86 million of these hidden codes and replaced them with real empty values. Forty-five percent of rows have no condition; we kept those rows and skip the blanks only where a chart needs that column.

[Presenter 2 · 0:25]
The label column had 104 spellings. Our function, sig group, checks keywords in order: conflicting first, then pathogenic without benign, benign without pathogenic, and uncertain. Order matters, because 'conflicting classifications of pathogenicity' contains the word pathogenic. We did the same to turn review status into zero-to-four stars.

[Presenter 2 · 0:30]
Then outliers. 111 review dates were before 1990, but ClinVar started in 2013, so we set them to empty. The IQR rule flags 22 percent of variants for having more than one lab, but those are real, popular variants, so we kept them. And the longest 0.1 percent of variants are left out of the length statistics only.

[Presenter 2 · 0:40]
Then machine learning. Can recorded features tell a pathogenic variant from a benign one? We compared three models on the same 200 thousand variants: a baseline that always says benign, logistic regression and a random forest. The baseline gets 79 percent accuracy but finds no harmful variants, so we compare AUC and recall instead. The random forest wins: AUC 0.81 against 0.78. Applied to the uncertain variants, about 60 thousand look strongly pathogenic: a review list, not a diagnosis.

[Presenter 2 · 0:30]

[Presenter 4 · 0:20]
Unknowns are growing faster than answers. Reviews jumped from about 33 thousand variants in 2017 to 1.36 million in 2025, and 877 thousand of the 2025 reviews were uncertain. Sequencing finds new variants faster than research can explain them.

[Presenter 4 · 0:15]
Most labels rest on one lab's opinion: 77 percent of variants come from a single lab, and only half a percent were checked by an expert panel. Before trusting a label, check its stars.

[Presenter 4 · 0:20]
Experts disagree most on breast-cancer genes: in BRCA2, one in four variants has conflicting labels. These are the most tested genes in the world, and more labs means more chances to disagree. That is exactly what our regression model found.

[Presenter 4 · 0:15]
Big DNA changes are easier to judge: 61 percent of deletions are pathogenic, while 57 percent of single-letter changes are uncertain. Our classifier agreed: the type of change was its most important feature.

[Presenter 4 · 0:15]
Which genes and conditions come up most? TTN, BRCA2 and NF1 lead the genes, and hereditary cancer leads the conditions by far. Big genes and heavily tested cancer genes collect the most harmful variants.

Machine-learning questions:
- Why compare against a baseline? It shows the models learned something: always saying 'benign' already scores 79% accuracy but finds no pathogenic variants.
- Why does the random forest still miss ~40% of pathogenic variants? Our features describe the kind of change, not what it does to the protein.
- Why not use review stars to predict conflict? The review status of a conflicting variant literally says 'conflicting', which would leak the answer.
